passages.speaker: Krishna
passages.listener: Dhritarashtra, Duryodhana and the Kaurava court
events: Krishna offers a settlement
Duryodhana refuses to part with a village
Krishna then works to build an alliance
passages.summary: Krishna goes to Hastinapura with a proposal small enough to be acceptable: five villages, not a kingdom. Duryodhana refuses even that, preferring a fight he believes he can win. The passage records the last moment at which the conflict could have been settled without blood, and it closes because one party would not concede anything at all.
passages.source_reference: Udyoga Parva — Krishna's embassy to Hastinapura
passages.verification_note: Episode identity and parva location verified against the standard 18-parva division. `summary` is an editorial rendering, not a quotation.

passages.speaker: Karna
events: Krishna reveals Karna's parentage
Krishna offers him the throne at Indraprastha
Karna refuses
passages.summary: Krishna tells Karna who he is and offers him everything the war would otherwise deny him. Karna answers that he has known for a long time, and that leaving now would make him ungrateful and untruthful: Duryodhana took him in when the world would not. He chooses loyalty to a benefactor over a claim he knows to be just.
passages.source_reference: Udyoga Parva — Karna's conversation with Krishna
passages.verification_note: Episode identity and parva location verified against the standard 18-parva division. `summary` is an editorial rendering, not a quotation.

passages.speaker: Vidura
events: Vidura tells the king he is complicit by omission
He warns that a king who cannot act should not hold the office
passages.summary: Vidura tells his brother that the fault is not only his son's: a ruler who knows what is happening, is told plainly, and still does nothing, is a party to it. He is blunt about consequences and does not soften the message to preserve the relationship. The text presents this as the correct behaviour of a counsellor, and shows it failing.
passages.source_reference: Udyoga Parva — Vidura's remonstrance to Dhritarashtra
passages.verification_note: Episode identity and parva location verified against the standard 18-parva division. `summary` is an editorial rendering, not a quotation.

passages.speaker: Draupadi
events: Draupadi recounts the wrong done to her
Krishna gives his word that her demand will be met
passages.summary: Draupadi tells Krishna exactly what was done and what remains owed. Krishna does not counsel acceptance; he promises that the debt will be paid. The scene establishes that her insistence was recorded as a legitimate claim rather than as an inability to move on.
passages.source_reference: Udyoga Parva — Draupadi and Krishna before the war
passages.verification_note: Episode identity and parva location verified against the standard 18-parva division. `summary` is an editorial rendering, not a quotation.

passages.section: Vidura on the duties of a counsellor
passages.speaker: Vidura
events: Vidura describes how advice should be given and how it should be received
passages.summary: Vidura distinguishes the person who flatters from the person who tells you what you do not want to hear, and argues that the second is the only one worth having near a throne. He also places a duty on the listener: advice that is heard and ignored is worse than never given.
passages.verification_note: Episode identity and parva location verified against the standard 18-parva division. `summary` is an editorial rendering, not a quotation.

passages.speaker: Arjuna
events: Arjuna lays down his bow
He names the people on the other side
passages.summary: Before the battle begins, Arjuna sees teachers, cousins, friends and grandfathers on the opposing side, and says that his limbs fail and his mouth is dry. He does not argue that war is wrong in general; he argues that he cannot do this particular thing to these particular people.
passages.verification_note: Bhagavad Gita location (Bhishma Parva, Adhyayas 25-42) verified. Text shown is an editorial summary of Arjuna's speech, not a quotation.

passages.section: Bhagavad Gita — on action and its fruits (2.47)
passages.speaker: Krishna
events: Krishna answers Arjuna's refusal to act
passages.original_text: karmaṇy evādhikāras te mā phaleṣu kadācana / mā karmaphalahetur bhūr mā te saṅgo 'stv akarmaṇi
passages.translation: You have a right to the work itself, never to its fruits. Let not the fruits of action be your motive, nor let your attachment be to inaction.
passages.summary: Krishna separates the domain in which a person actually has authority — the action — from the outcome, which depends on many things they do not control. The instruction is not to stop caring about results; it is to stop making them the thing you are acting for.
passages.verification_note: Verse reference verified against the standard Bhagavad Gita numbering; Sanskrit is IAST transliteration and the English is a conventional rendering, not a scholarly translation.

passages.speaker: Krishna
events: Krishna defines steadiness
passages.original_text: yoga-sthah kuru karmāṇi saṅgaṁ tyaktvā dhanañjaya / siddhy-asiddhyoḥ samo bhūtvā samatvaṁ yoga ucyate
passages.translation: Standing firm in yoga, perform your actions, abandoning attachment — remaining the same in success and in failure. This evenness of mind is called yoga.
passages.summary: Steadiness is defined as continuing to act while treating favourable and unfavourable outcomes as equally acceptable. The claim is about how to hold an outcome, not about whether it matters.
passages.verification_note: Verse reference verified against the standard Bhagavad Gita numbering; Sanskrit is IAST transliteration and the English is a conventional rendering, not a scholarly translation.

passages.speaker: Krishna
events: Krishna compares one's own duty with another's
passages.original_text: śreyān svadharmo viguṇaḥ paradharmāt svanuṣṭhitāt / svadharme nidhanaṁ śreyaḥ paradharmo bhayāvahaḥ
passages.translation: Better is one's own duty, though imperfectly performed, than the duty of another well performed. Death in one's own duty is better; another's duty is fraught with danger.
passages.summary: Krishna argues that the work you are actually placed in is safer ground than work that belongs to someone else and suits you better. The verse is often quoted as a defence of staying put; in context it is an argument about which obligations are genuinely yours to discharge.
passages.verification_note: Verse reference verified against the standard Bhagavad Gita numbering; Sanskrit is IAST transliteration and the English is a conventional rendering, not a scholarly translation.

passages.speaker: Krishna
events: Krishna addresses Arjuna's grief over change and loss
passages.original_text: mātra-sparśās tu kaunteya śītoṣṇa-sukha-duḥkhadāḥ / āgamāpāyino 'nityās tāṁs titikṣasvā bhārata
passages.translation: Contacts of the senses with their objects, son of Kunti, give rise to cold and heat, pleasure and pain. They come and go and are impermanent; endure them bravely.
passages.summary: Krishna names the unpleasant sensations precisely rather than dismissing them, and locates them as things that arrive and depart. The counsel is endurance with clear seeing, not denial that the experience is real.
passages.verification_note: Verse reference verified against the standard Bhagavad Gita numbering; Sanskrit is IAST transliteration and the English is a conventional rendering, not a scholarly translation.

passages.speaker: Krishna
events: Krishna argues against grief for those who will die
passages.original_text: na jāyate mriyate vā kadācin nāyaṁ bhūtvā bhavitā vā na bhūyaḥ / ajo nityaḥ śāśvato 'yaṁ purāṇo na hanyate hanyamāne śarīre
passages.translation: The self is never born, nor does it die. Unborn, eternal, everlasting and ancient, it is not slain when the body is slain.
passages.summary: Krishna reframes Arjuna's grief by changing what he believes he is looking at. The passage is often quoted for consolation; in context it is a premise he needs Arjuna to accept before the next argument can be heard.
passages.verification_note: Verse reference verified against the standard Bhagavad Gita numbering; Sanskrit is IAST transliteration and the English is a conventional rendering, not a scholarly translation.

passages.section: Bhagavad Gita — birth and death as unavoidable (2.27)
passages.speaker: Krishna
events: Krishna tells Arjuna not to grieve for what cannot be avoided
passages.original_text: jātasya hi dhruvo mṛtyur dhruvaṁ janma mṛtasya ca / tasmād aparihārye 'rthe na te śokaḥ kartumaṅyasi
passages.translation: Whatever is born is sure to die, and whatever dies is sure to be born again. Therefore you should not grieve for what is unavoidable.
passages.summary: A short, hard statement about what cannot be prevented. It is directed at a specific person about a specific fear, and it is not offered as a general licence to stop caring.
passages.verification_note: Verse reference verified against the standard Bhagavad Gita numbering; Sanskrit is IAST transliteration and the English is a conventional rendering, not a scholarly translation.

passages.section: Bhagavad Gita — lift yourself by yourself (6.5)
passages.speaker: Krishna
events: Krishna speaks on self-reliance in discipline
passages.translation: A person should lift themselves by themselves; they should not let themselves sink. The self alone is the friend of the self, and the self alone is its own enemy.
passages.summary: Krishna makes the individual responsible for their own steadiness: the same person can be the support or the obstacle. The instruction is paired with the warning that a person who has not made themselves their ally will be defeated by themselves.
passages.verification_note: Verse reference verified against the standard Bhagavad Gita numbering; the English is a conventional rendering, not a scholarly translation, and no Sanskrit is quoted here.

passages.speaker: Krishna
events: Krishna explains why he appears in each age
passages.original_text: yadā yadā hi dharmasya glānir bhavati bhārata / abhyutthānam adharmasya tadātmānaṁ sṛjāmy aham
passages.translation: Whenever there is a decline of dharma and a rise of disorder, then I manifest myself. For the protection of the good, for the destruction of the wicked, and for the establishment of dharma, I come into being age after age.
passages.summary: Krishna gives a reason for intervention: appearance is tied to a measurable condition rather than to preference. The verse is routinely quoted as a general claim; in context it is offered to explain why a war of this scale is not something he is preventing.
passages.verification_note: Verse reference verified against the standard Bhagavad Gita numbering; Sanskrit is IAST transliteration and the English is a conventional rendering, not a scholarly translation.

passages.speaker: Krishna
events: Krishna closes his teaching
passages.original_text: sarva-dharmān parityajya mām ekaṁ śaraṇaṁ vraja / ahaṁ tvāṁ sarva-pāpebhyo mokṣayiṣyāmi mā śucaḥ
passages.translation: Abandoning all dharmas, take refuge in me alone. I will free you from all evils; do not grieve.
passages.summary: The last instruction of the discourse, and the most difficult: it asks the listener to set down the very framework he has been reasoning with. Readings of it differ sharply — as surrender, as a claim about the limits of rule-following, or as an assurance rather than an instruction.
passages.verification_note: Verse reference verified against the standard Bhagavad Gita numbering; Sanskrit is IAST transliteration and the English is a conventional rendering, not a scholarly translation.

passages.section: Bhishma's oath and his refusal to fight Shikhandi
passages.speaker: Bhishma
events: Bhishma declares he will not fight Shikhandi
He explains the conditions under which he will fight
passages.summary: Bhishma tells the Kaurava court in advance that he will not raise a weapon against the man born to be his undoing. He fights for the throne he swore to protect while knowing the terms on which he will lose. The text lets him state his own conditions and then shows the cost of them being met exactly.
passages.source_reference: Bhishma Parva — Bhishma's declaration before the war
passages.verification_note: Episode identity verified against the standard 18-parva division; `summary` is an editorial rendering, not a quotation.

passages.speaker: narrator / Bhishma
events: Shikhandi is placed in front
Bhishma is struck down and chooses the time of his death
passages.summary: The commander who has been on the field since before either army was born is brought down by the exact combination he named beforehand. He lies on the shafts and later chooses when to let go. The scene is the text's picture of a person bound by their own commitments, meeting the consequence in full view of everyone who advised against it.
passages.source_reference: Bhishma Parva — the fall of Bhishma
passages.verification_note: Episode identity verified against the standard 18-parva division; `summary` is an editorial rendering, not a quotation.
